record.paper_title: Recent Results and Open Problems in Evolutionary Multiobjective Optimization
record.original_question: Which structural features make a multi-objective optimization problem difficult for a multi-objective evolutionary algorithm, and which algorithmic features should a MOEA have to solve real-world problems or meaningful subclasses efficiently?

evidence.quote: What makes a problem difficult for a MOEA?
we do not know what features are desirable in a MOEA

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A multi-objective optimization problem (MOP) is a tuple (X, f) where X is a search space (e.g. a subset of {0,1}^n, R^n, or a combinatorial set) and f = (f_1, ..., f_m) : X -> R^m is a vector of m >= 2 objective functions. For x, y in X, x dominates y if f_i(x) <= f_i(y) for every i and f(x) != f(y). The Pareto set is the set of non-dominated points of X, and the Pareto front is its image under f. A multi-objective evolutionary algorithm (MOEA) is a randomized iterative procedure that maintains a population P_t ⊆ X, updates it via variation operators (mutation, recombination) and selection operators (based on dominance, diversity measures such as crowding distance or hypervolume contribution), and aims to produce a population whose image approximates the Pareto front.

Provide a rigorous theory addressing the following two linked questions:

(a) Identify and formally characterize the structural features of a multi-objective optimization problem (X, f) — for instance, properties of the Pareto front geometry (connectedness, convexity, dimension), the structure of the level sets of the f_i, the ruggedness or epistasis of the objective landscape, the cardinality and distribution of the Pareto set, scaling and conflict among objectives, presence of plateaus, deceptive regions, or many-objective phenomena (m large) — that provably make (X, f) hard for any MOEA in a precise complexity-theoretic sense (e.g. super-polynomial expected runtime to reach a (1+ε)-approximation of the Pareto front, or to cover it under a given indicator).

(b) Identify and prove which algorithmic features (representation, variation operators, selection mechanisms, archive strategies, diversity maintenance, use of indicators such as hypervolume or IGD, adaptive parameter control, etc.) a MOEA must possess in order to solve, in expected polynomial time, either practically relevant real-world MOPs or well-defined nontrivial subclasses of MOPs characterized by the structural features identified in (a).

The goal is to obtain matching hardness and tractability results that together delineate, in a problem-independent way, both what makes MOPs hard for MOEAs and what algorithmic ingredients are necessary and sufficient for efficient MOEA-based solution.
artifact.status_search_result: This is a broadly stated foundational open problem in evolutionary multiobjective optimization. While considerable progress has been made on runtime analyses of specific MOEAs (e.g. SEMO, GSEMO, NSGA-II) on benchmark problems, no general theory characterizes problem difficulty for MOEAs nor identifies necessary/sufficient algorithmic features for solving real-world MOPs. Recent surveys and runtime-analysis works continue to list these questions as open.
